exercises.prompt: Implement count_up(n) as a GENERATOR that yields the integers 0, 1, 2, …, n − 1 in order — one at a time, using yield rather than building and returning a list. list(count_up(3)) is [0, 1, 2]. count_up(0) yields nothing, so list(count_up(0)) is []. Assume n is a non-negative integer.
hints: A generator produces values lazily: instead of return, it uses yield inside a loop, handing back one value per iteration.
Loop over range(n) — which counts 0, 1, …, n − 1 — and yield each number.
for i in range(n): yield i — because range(n) stops before n and is empty for n = 0, list(count_up(0)) is [] and next(count_up(5)) is 0, the first value pulled.

exercises.prompt: Implement count_down(n) as a GENERATOR that yields the integers n, n − 1, …, down to 1, in that descending order, using yield. It stops before 0. list(count_down(3)) is [3, 2, 1]. count_down(0) yields nothing, so list(count_down(0)) is []. Assume n is a non-negative integer.
hints: This is count_up run backwards: yield the largest value first and work down to 1, stopping before 0.
range(n, 0, -1) counts down from n to 1 (the stop value 0 is excluded); yield each step.
for i in range(n, 0, -1): yield i — the descending range makes list(count_down(3)) come out [3, 2, 1], not [1, 2, 3], and yields nothing when n is 0.

exercises.prompt: Implement evens_up_to(n) as a GENERATOR that yields the even numbers 0, 2, 4, … from 0 up to but NOT including n, in order, using yield. list(evens_up_to(10)) is [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] — 10 itself is excluded. list(evens_up_to(0)) is []. Assume n is a non-negative integer.
hints: You want every second number starting at 0, stopping once you reach n — so the value n never appears.
range(0, n, 2) does exactly that: it starts at 0, steps by 2, and stops before n.
for i in range(0, n, 2): yield i — because the stop is exclusive, evens_up_to(10) ends at 8 (not 10) and evens_up_to(2) is just [0].

exercises.prompt: Implement take(n, xs) as a GENERATOR that yields the first n elements of the list xs, in order, using yield — and stops early once it has yielded n of them. list(take(2, [10, 20, 30])) is [10, 20]. If n is 0, it yields nothing; if n is larger than the list, it yields the whole list. list(take(5, [1, 2])) is [1, 2].
hints: Walk xs and yield elements, but keep count so you can stop the moment you have handed back n of them.
enumerate(xs) pairs each element with its index i; once i reaches n, stop with a bare return so no more values are yielded.
for i, x in enumerate(xs): if i >= n: return; else yield x — stopping at i >= n makes take(2, [10, 20, 30]) yield [10, 20], and take(0, …) yields nothing at all.

exercises.prompt: Implement repeat_each(xs) as a GENERATOR that yields every element of the list xs TWICE in a row, in order, using yield. list(repeat_each([1, 2])) is [1, 1, 2, 2] — each element appears back-to-back, not [1, 2, 1, 2]. An empty list yields nothing, so list(repeat_each([])) is [].
hints: For each element you need two yields, one right after the other, before moving on to the next element.
Inside a loop over xs, yield x and then yield x again — the second yield fires before the loop advances.
for x in xs: yield x; yield x — yielding twice per element keeps the copies adjacent, so [1, 2] becomes [1, 1, 2, 2], not [1, 2, 1, 2].
